description: Negative feedback control of blood glucose by insulin and glucagon, diabetes, and thermoregulation.
hero_image_caption: The pancreas monitors blood glucose and releases insulin or glucagon to restore balance.
content_html:
What is Homeostasis?

Homeostasis is the maintenance of a stable internal environment (B3.3a). This matters because enzymes and metabolic reactions work within narrow ranges of temperature, pH, blood glucose and water balance. If any of these drift too far from the optimum, cell processes slow down or stop — potentially with fatal consequences.

All homeostatic systems share the same three-part architecture: receptors detect deviations from the normal level, a coordination centre (such as the brain or pancreas) processes the information and sends instructions, and effectors (muscles or glands) carry out the response. The system operates through negative feedback: once conditions return to normal, the response is switched off.

Key Fact

Homeostasis maintains a stable internal environment using negative feedback. Every control system has three components: receptor (detects change), coordination centre (processes information), effector (produces the corrective response).

Blood Glucose Control

Blood glucose concentration is monitored continuously by the pancreas (B3.3b–c). When blood glucose rises after a carbohydrate-rich meal, specialised beta cells in the pancreas detect the increase and release insulin into the blood. Insulin has two effects: it causes body cells (especially muscles and liver) to absorb glucose from the blood, and it stimulates the liver to convert excess glucose into glycogen for storage. Both effects lower blood glucose back to normal.

When blood glucose falls — for example, during exercise or between meals — alpha cells in the pancreas detect the drop and release glucagon. Glucagon stimulates the liver to break glycogen back down into glucose (glycogenolysis) and release it into the blood, raising glucose back to normal. The opposing actions of insulin (lowering glucose) and glucagon (raising glucose) form a classic negative feedback loop that maintains blood glucose within a safe, narrow range (B3.3b, Higher Tier).

Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune condition: the immune system destroys the insulin-producing beta cells in the pancreas. Without insulin, blood glucose rises dangerously after eating. Treatment requires regular insulin injections (or an insulin pump) combined with careful monitoring of blood glucose and carbohydrate intake. It usually develops in childhood or early adulthood and cannot be prevented (B3.3d).

Type 2 diabetes develops when body cells become resistant to insulin — they no longer respond appropriately, so blood glucose stays elevated even though the pancreas may still produce insulin. It is strongly associated with obesity, a sedentary lifestyle and genetic factors. Treatment typically involves a controlled diet (limiting refined carbohydrates and sugars), regular exercise, and sometimes medication. Type 2 can often be prevented or managed through lifestyle changes, unlike Type 1 (B3.3d).

Key Fact

Type 1 diabetes: the pancreas cannot produce insulin (autoimmune; treated with insulin injections). Type 2 diabetes: body cells become resistant to insulin (often linked to obesity; treated with diet and exercise, sometimes medication).

Temperature Regulation

Core body temperature in humans is maintained at approximately 37 °C by the thermoregulatory centre in the brain (B3.3c). It receives signals from thermoreceptors in the skin (detecting external temperature) and from receptors monitoring blood temperature in the brain itself. Together these provide a complete picture of the body’s thermal state, allowing the coordination centre to activate appropriate effectors.

When the body is too hot, three main effector responses lower temperature. Vasodilation: blood vessels near the skin surface widen, so more warm blood flows close to the skin and more heat is radiated away. Sweating: sweat glands release sweat onto the skin; water in sweat evaporates, removing heat energy from the skin (evaporative cooling). Body hairs lying flat: erector muscles relax, so hairs lie flat against the skin, reducing the insulating layer of trapped air.

Vasoconstriction: blood vessels near the skin surface narrow, diverting blood away from the skin and reducing heat loss by radiation. Shivering: skeletal muscles contract rapidly and repeatedly; the increased metabolic activity generates heat that warms the body. Body hairs standing on end: erector muscles contract, raising hairs and trapping a thicker insulating layer of air close to the skin (more effective in furry animals than in humans).

Both sets of responses illustrate negative feedback — once body temperature returns to 37 °C, the thermoreceptors detect the change and the effector responses are switched off. This cyclical on-off control is what keeps core temperature within a narrow, safe range.

It is worth noting that the nervous and endocrine systems work together in thermoregulation. The nervous system sends rapid signals to sweat glands and erector muscles (which raise body hairs), while hormones such as adrenaline can also boost metabolic heat production in emergency cold exposure. The skin acts as the primary interface with the environment — its rich blood supply and large surface area make it the key organ for heat exchange. Evaporative cooling via sweat is particularly important during physical exercise, when the body can generate large amounts of metabolic heat through increased muscle respiration.
exam_tip_html: For blood glucose questions, be precise: insulin is released when glucose is high and causes cells to absorb glucose and the liver to store it as glycogen. Glucagon (Higher Tier) is released when glucose is low and causes the liver to break glycogen back into glucose. A common error is confusing glycogen (storage form) with glucagon (the hormone). For temperature regulation, describe the mechanism, not just the outcome: say ‘vasodilation allows more blood to flow close to the skin surface, increasing heat loss by radiation’, rather than just ‘more blood goes to the skin’. For Type 1 vs Type 2 diabetes questions, always state the cause and the treatment for both.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Homeostasis maintains a stable internal environment using receptors, coordination centres and effectors working through negative feedback. The pancreas controls blood glucose: insulin lowers it (glucose absorbed, glycogen formed), glucagon raises it (glycogen broken down) — Higher Tier.
  • Type 1 diabetes: autoimmune destruction of beta cells, no insulin produced, treated with injections. Type 2 diabetes: insulin resistance, lifestyle-linked, treated with diet, exercise and medication.
  • Thermoregulation keeps core temperature near 37 °C: too hot → vasodilation + sweating + hairs flat; too cold → vasoconstriction + shivering + hairs raised. Both are negative feedback responses.

practice_questions.text: Name the two hormones produced by the pancreas that control blood glucose concentration.
practice_questions.marks: A: Insulin and glucagon (1 mark — both required for the mark).

practice_questions.text: Describe what happens in the body when blood glucose concentration rises above the normal level.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: The pancreas releases insulin into the blood (1); insulin causes body cells to take up glucose and the liver to convert excess glucose to glycogen, lowering blood glucose back to normal (1). Emerging: Vague — e.g. 'insulin is made and lowers glucose' without identifying where glucose goes.

practice_questions.text: Explain how vasoconstriction helps the body conserve heat when core temperature drops.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Blood vessels near the skin surface narrow (vasoconstrict) (1); less warm blood flows close to the skin surface (1); so less heat is lost to the surroundings by radiation, conserving heat in the body's core (1). Secure: Two points logically linked. Developing: States 'vessels narrow so less blood goes to skin' but does not explain the effect on heat loss. Emerging: Confused — e.g. 'vasoconstriction makes blood hotter'.

practice_questions.text: A student measures their blood glucose at four time points: fasting (5.0 mmol/L), 30 min after a meal (8.4 mmol/L), 60 min after a meal (6.9 mmol/L) and 120 min after a meal (5.1 mmol/L). Calculate the percentage decrease in blood glucose between 30 min and 120 min. Show your working and give your answer to 1 decimal place.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Decrease = 8.4 − 5.1 = 3.3 mmol/L (1); percentage decrease = (3.3 ÷ 8.4) × 100 (1) = 39.28...% (1); rounded correctly to 39.3% (1). Penalise missing % symbol or incorrect rounding. Secure: Correct method with arithmetic error in one step (max 3 marks).

practice_questions.text: Explain why a person with Type 1 diabetes requires insulin injections but a person with Type 2 diabetes may be able to manage their condition without injections.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: In Type 1 diabetes, the immune system destroys insulin-producing beta cells so no insulin is produced; without injections, blood glucose cannot be controlled (1). In Type 2 diabetes, the pancreas may still produce insulin but body cells are resistant to it (1); lifestyle changes such as diet and exercise can reduce insulin resistance and improve glucose uptake without the need for injections (1). Secure: Two of the three points. Developing: Distinguishes the two types but does not explain why injections are only needed in Type 1. Emerging: Confuses the two types.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the importance of negative feedback in maintaining blood glucose homeostasis. In your answer, explain what would happen if negative feedback mechanisms failed, with reference to diabetes as an example.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Negative feedback ensures that any deviation from the set point (normal blood glucose) triggers a corrective response that brings glucose back to normal — preventing it from rising too high (hyperglycaemia) or falling too low (hypoglycaemia), both of which are dangerous. Without insulin (as in Type 1 diabetes), blood glucose can rise after eating and cells are deprived of glucose for respiration, leading to fatigue, organ damage and, if untreated, diabetic ketoacidosis. Without glucagon (Higher Tier), blood glucose could fall dangerously, impairing brain function since the brain relies almost entirely on glucose. The fact that two opposing hormones (insulin and glucagon) are involved makes the system more responsive and precise than a single-hormone system. A clear evaluative conclusion on why negative feedback is essential for survival. Secure: Four well-made points. Developing: Two points, limited evaluation. Emerging: One relevant point.

knowledge_checks.q: Which cells in the pancreas release insulin when blood glucose is too high?
What happens to blood vessels near the skin when the body is too hot?
options: They vasodilate so more heat is lost by radiation
They vasodilate to produce more sweat

knowledge_checks.q: When blood glucose is too low, the pancreas releases _____, which stimulates the liver to convert glycogen back into glucose.
Type 2 diabetes develops when body cells become _____ to insulin, so blood glucose remains elevated.
Match each homeostatic response to the situation that triggers it.
right: Body temperature too low — muscles contract rapidly to generate heat
Body temperature too high — evaporation of water removes heat
Body temperature too high — more blood flows to skin surface

flashcard_questions.q: What are the three components of every homeostatic control system?
flashcard_questions.a: Receptor (detects change), coordination centre (processes information), effector (produces response)

flashcard_questions.q: What does insulin do to blood glucose?
flashcard_questions.a: Lowers it — causes cells to absorb glucose and liver to convert glucose to glycogen

flashcard_questions.q: What does glucagon do to blood glucose?
flashcard_questions.a: Raises it — stimulates the liver to break glycogen back into glucose and release it into the blood
An insoluble polysaccharide stored in the liver and muscles that acts as a short-term glucose reserve

flashcard_questions.q: Why does Type 1 diabetes require insulin injections?
flashcard_questions.a: The immune system destroys beta cells so the pancreas cannot produce insulin

flashcard_questions.q: How does Type 2 diabetes differ from Type 1 in its cause?
flashcard_questions.a: Body cells become resistant to insulin; the pancreas may still produce insulin but cells do not respond properly

flashcard_questions.q: What is vasodilation and when does it occur?
flashcard_questions.a: Widening of skin blood vessels when the body is too hot, allowing more heat to be lost by radiation

flashcard_questions.q: How does sweating cool the body?
flashcard_questions.a: Water in sweat evaporates from the skin, removing heat energy from the body (evaporative cooling)

flashcard_questions.q: What is vasoconstriction and when does it occur?
flashcard_questions.a: Narrowing of skin blood vessels when the body is too cold, reducing heat loss by radiation
The maintenance of a stable internal environment using negative feedback

flashcard_questions.q: Why is maintaining body temperature near 37°C important?
flashcard_questions.a: Enzymes work at their optimum rate at this temperature; too hot or too cold slows or stops metabolic reactions

glossary_terms.definition: The regulation of the internal conditions of a cell or organism to maintain a stable internal environment, in response to both internal and external changes.
Cells or organs that detect changes in the internal or external environment and send information to a coordination centre.
Muscles or glands that carry out the corrective response, restoring conditions to the set point.
A control mechanism where the output of a system feeds back to reverse the original change, keeping conditions within a narrow range around a set point.
A hormone released by beta cells in the pancreas that lowers blood glucose by stimulating cells to absorb glucose and the liver to convert glucose to glycogen for storage.
A hormone released by alpha cells in the pancreas that raises blood glucose by stimulating the liver to convert stored glycogen back into glucose and release it into the blood.
An insoluble polysaccharide stored in the liver and muscles that acts as a short-term glucose reserve.
An autoimmune condition in which the immune system destroys insulin-producing beta cells in the pancreas, resulting in an inability to regulate blood glucose without insulin injections.
A condition in which the body's cells become resistant to insulin, so blood glucose remains elevated despite insulin being produced; strongly linked to obesity and a sedentary lifestyle.
The widening of blood vessels near the skin surface, increasing blood flow to the skin so more heat is lost to the surroundings by radiation.
The narrowing of blood vessels near the skin surface, reducing blood flow to the skin and conserving heat in the body's core.
